payload.question: Does intermittent fasting improve insulin sensitivity in adults with prediabetes?

payload.h0: In adults with prediabetes, 12 weeks of 16:8 time-restricted eating vs a usual-meal-timing control with matched total caloric intake produces no difference in change in insulin sensitivity.
payload.statement: In adults with prediabetes, 12 weeks of 16:8 time-restricted eating improves insulin sensitivity (estimand: mean between-group difference in change in HOMA-IR, with clamp substudy; unit: participant) compared with a usual-timing eating pattern at equal caloric intake — i.e., fasting timing has an intake-independent effect.

payload.h0: At equal weight loss, intermittent fasting and continuous energy restriction produce the same change in insulin sensitivity; fasting confers no weight-loss-independent benefit.
payload.statement: Any insulin-sensitivity benefit of intermittent fasting in adults with prediabetes (estimand: between-group difference in change in HOMA-IR per kg weight lost, and weight-loss-adjusted difference; unit: participant) is fully explained by greater energy deficit and weight loss — i.e., fasting has no independent mechanism beyond calorie restriction (simpler-mechanism rival).

payload.h0: Adjusting for objectively measured sleep duration/quality, late-night energy intake, and physical activity eliminates any between-group difference in insulin-sensitivity change attributed to intermittent fasting.
payload.statement: Apparent insulin-sensitivity gains from intermittent fasting in adults with prediabetes (estimand: direct effect of fasting assignment on HOMA-IR change not mediated through sleep, meal-timing, and activity; unit: participant) are confounded/mediated by co-behavioural changes — improved sleep, elimination of late-night eating, and altered activity — rather than by fasting physiology itself (confounder rival).

payload.claim: Across 14 randomized trials (n=1101 adults with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes), intermittent fasting reduced body weight (WMD -4.56 kg), HbA1c (WMD -0.81%), fasting glucose (WMD -0.36 mmol/L), total cholesterol and triglycerides versus control/calorie-restriction comparators.
payload.limitation: Meta-analysis pooling prediabetes with type 2 diabetes; IF protocols and comparators (control diet and/or calorie restriction) mixed; trial durations and adherence vary.
payload.source_excerpt: Abstract Aim To perform a meta‐analysis to investigate the effects of intermittent fasting (IF), as compared with either a control diet (CON) and/or calorie restriction (CR), on body composition and cardiometabolic health in individuals with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes (T2D). Methods PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched from their inception to March 2024 to identify original randomized trials with parallel or crossover designs that studied the effects of IF on body composition and cardiometabolic health. Weighted mean differences (WMDs) or standardized mean differences with 95%
payload.title: The effects of intermittent fasting on body composition and cardiometabolic health in adults with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes: A systematic review and meta‐analysis

payload.claim: In adults with prediabetes (HbA1c 40-50 mmol/mol), 12 weeks of 5:2 intermittent fasting (2 days/week at 600-650 kcal/day) reduced HbA1c from 43 to 41 mmol/mol (p<0.001) across the combined fasting arms.
payload.limitation: Small feasibility trial (26 completers of 33 enrolled); all participants fasted so no non-fasting control; concurrent probiotic-vs-placebo randomization confounds attribution to fasting alone.
payload.source_excerpt: Both intermittent fasting and specific probiotics have shown promise in improving glucose tolerance with a potential for synergistic effects through alterations to gut microbiota. In this randomized, double-blinded, two-arm feasibility study, we investigated whether intermittent fasting, supplemented with Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus HN001 probiotic, reduces HbA1c in individuals with prediabetes. payload.title: PROFAST: A Randomized Trial Assessing the Effects of Intermittent Fasting and Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus Probiotic among People with Prediabetes

payload.claim: In 72 adults with impaired fasting glucose randomized to TRE plus behavioral-economics intervention, TRE alone, or usual care, mean body weight, fasting glucose, HbA1c, fasting insulin and lipids did not significantly differ among groups; only the per-protocol (complier) analysis showed lower fasting glucose, HbA1c and fasting insulin with TRE versus usual care.
payload.limitation: Small single trial (n=72, three arms); intention-to-treat result null with benefit only in compliers, so sensitive to adherence; short-term surrogate outcomes only.
payload.source_excerpt: This randomized controlled trial is aimed at assessing the efficacy of combining time-restricted eating (TRE) with behavioral economic (BE) interventions and comparing it to TRE alone and to the usual care for reducing fasting plasma glucose (FPG), hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), and other cardiometabolic risk factors among patients with impaired fasting glucose (IFG). Seventy-two IFG patients aged 18-65 years were randomly allocated for TRE with BE interventions (26 patients), TRE alone (24 patients), or usual care (22 patients). Mean FPG, HbA1c, and other cardiometabolic risk factors among the three
payload.title: Efficacy of Time-Restricted Eating and Behavioral Economic Intervention in Reducing Fasting Plasma Glucose, HbA1c, and Cardiometabolic Risk Factors in Patients with Impaired Fasting Glucose: A Randomized Controlled Trial

payload.claim: Across 28 randomized trials of TRE, alternate-day fasting, or 5:2 diets (2-52 weeks), intermittent energy restriction and continuous energy restriction produced comparable changes in body weight (WMD -0.42 kg, p=0.132) and fat mass, with slightly greater waist and fat-free-mass reductions under intermittent restriction.
payload.limitation: Population was healthy adults rather than prediabetes specifically; energy intakes were comparable in only 17 of 28 trials (lower in intermittent arms in 5, unreported in 6); protocols and durations heterogeneous.
payload.source_excerpt: The interest in intermittent energy restriction (IER) diets as weight loss approach is increasing. Different IER protocols exist, including time-restricted eating (TRE), alternate-day fasting (ADF), and the 5:2 diet. This meta-analysis compared the effects of these IER diets to continuous energy restriction (CER) on anthropometrics and cardiometabolic risk markers in healthy adults. Twenty-eight trials were identified that studied TRE (k=7), ADF (k=10), or the 5:2 diet (k=11) for 2 to 52 weeks. Energy intakes between intervention groups within a study were comparable (17 trials), lower in IER
payload.title: Effects of Intermittent Energy Restriction Compared with Those of Continuous Energy Restriction on Body Composition and Cardiometabolic Risk Markers – A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials in Adults

payload.claim: Reviewing clinical trials through June 2021, time-restricted eating lowered fasting and postprandial glucose, mean 24-hour glucose and glycemic excursions, reduced fasting insulin and improved insulin sensitivity in a range of trials, while a number of studies found adverse or no effects on glycemic and lipid traits.
payload.limitation: Narrative review, not a quantitative meta-analysis; pools heterogeneous TRE windows, populations and outcome measures, so prediabetes-specific effect sizes cannot be isolated.
payload.source_excerpt: Time-restricted eating (TRE), a dietary approach limiting the daily eating window, has attracted increasing attention in media and research. The eating behavior in our modern society is often characterized by prolonged and erratic daily eating patterns, which might be associated with increased risk of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular diseases. In contrast, recent evidence suggests that TRE might support weight loss, improve cardiometabolic health, and overall wellbeing, but the data are controversial. payload.title: Time Restricted Eating: A Dietary Strategy to Prevent and Treat Metabolic Disturbances

payload.comparator: Usual-timing control: same prescribed isocaloric diet (weight-maintenance energy needs, dietitian-prescribed, no deficit) spread over ≥12-h eating window with 3 meals + optional snacks; both arms receive identical diet composition counselling and contact time.
payload.cost_estimate: Planning assumptions: ~12 months, roughly $350k–$600k (assumption: staff, dietitian support, assays, clamp substudy, actigraphy/CGM); negligible compute beyond standard statistics.
payload.design: Two-arm parallel randomised controlled trial in adults with prediabetes (ADA criteria, assumption). Units: participants. Arms: (A) 16:8 time-restricted eating (e.g., 08:00–16:00 window, water/unsweetened beverages outside) with isocaloric weight-maintenance prescription; (B) usual-timing control. Randomisation stratified by site/sex/baseline HOMA-IR (assumption). Timing: 2-week run-in with weight-stability check, then 12-week intervention. Blinding: participants/personnel unblinded to diet; outcome assessors and laboratory staff blinded; prespecified analysis plan. Adherence monitored by time-stamped meal photos/app logs plus continuous glucose monitoring wear (assumption). Weight monitored to confirm isocaloric maintenance; protocol-defined rescue if weight drifts.
payload.falsifier: Q1 is refuted if the between-group difference in HOMA-IR change (TRE minus control) at 12 weeks is statistically indistinguishable from zero, or its confidence interval excludes the smallest important effect: a 15% relative improvement / 0.5-unit absolute HOMA-IR difference (assumption for smallest important effect, no citation). A null clamp-substudy result in the same direction corroborates refutation.
payload.measurements: Primary outcome: change from baseline to 12 weeks in HOMA-IR from fasting glucose and insulin drawn after a standardised prior-day diet and overnight fast, assayed in a central blinded laboratory. Secondary/confirmatory: hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp or frequently sampled test in a consenting substudy; fasting glucose, HbA1c, body weight, actigraphy sleep, and adherence logs as covariates.
payload.risks: Threats: non-adherence and timing crossover; compensatory overeating breaking isocaloric match; differential dropout; regression to the mean; seasonal effects. Ethics/safety: hypoglycaemia risk (low in prediabetes without glucose-lowering drugs, assumption — exclude insulin/sulfonylurea users); disordered-eating screening and monitoring; exclusion of pregnant people and history of eating disorders; data-safety monitoring for excessive weight loss.
payload.sample_size: Target ~140 randomised (70/arm, assumption) to detect the smallest important effect above with 80% power at two-sided alpha 0.05, allowing ~15% attrition. All inputs (baseline mean/SD of HOMA-IR change, correlation, attrition) are assumptions; justification is power for the prespecified smallest important effect, not an observed effect.
payload.title: P1 isocaloric TRE vs usual-timing RCT for Q1

payload.comparator: Continuous energy restriction (CER) control: daily ~25% deficit (assumption) with standard meal timing (≥12-h window), matched to the IF arm on prescribed weekly energy deficit, macronutrient targets, dietitian contact, and activity advice.
payload.cost_estimate: Planning assumptions: ~14 months, roughly $400k–$700k (assumption: longer follow-up, dietitian delivery, Doubly-labelled-water or intake biomarkers in subsample, assays); minimal compute.
payload.design: Two-arm parallel randomised trial in adults with prediabetes. Units: participants. Arms: (A) intermittent fasting with deficit — 5:2 (two non-consecutive very-low-energy days/week) or 16:8 TRE plus prescribed deficit; (B) continuous daily energy restriction with matched prescribed weekly deficit. Randomisation stratified by baseline weight/HOMA-IR (assumption). Timing: 2-week weight-stable run-in, 12-week weight-loss phase, 12-week maintenance follow-up (total 24 weeks, assumption). Blinding: participants unblinded; assessors/laboratory blinded. Energy prescription and counselling time equalised; adherence via food records, meal-timing logs, and weight trajectories; prespecified weight-loss-adjusted (ANCOVA/mediation) analysis to separate fasting effect from weight-loss effect.
payload.falsifier: Q2 (weight-loss-only explanation) is refuted if, after adjustment for weight change (and in per-kg-lost analysis), the IF arm shows a larger HOMA-IR improvement than CER exceeding the smallest important residual effect: ≥0.4-unit HOMA-IR or ≥10% relative difference at equal weight loss (assumption, no citation). Q2 is supported (not refuted) if unadjusted differences vanish after weight-loss adjustment with the adjusted confidence interval excluding that residual effect.
payload.measurements: Primary outcome: change in HOMA-IR at 12 and 24 weeks (central blinded fasting assays after standardised fast), analysed unadjusted and adjusted for concurrent weight change; co-primary metric: HOMA-IR change per kg weight lost. Supporting: body weight, waist, HbA1c, fasting insulin/glucose, adherence and energy-intake biomarkers in a subsample.
payload.risks: Threats: unequal achieved (vs prescribed) deficits confounding the comparison; differential adherence/dropout; compensatory eating on feast days; physical-activity changes; measurement error in intake. Ethics/safety: as in P1 plus monitoring for excessive restriction, hypoglycaemia in those on glucose-lowering drugs (exclude or co-manage, assumption), and disordered eating; prespecified stopping and referral criteria.
payload.sample_size: Target ~180 randomised (90/arm, assumption) to power both the unadjusted comparison and the weight-loss-adjusted ANCOVA for the residual effect above at 80% power, alpha 0.05, allowing ~20% attrition. Variance, weight-loss, and attrition inputs are assumptions; final size to be set by a blinded sample-size re-estimation (assumption).
payload.title: P2 deficit-matched IF vs continuous restriction RCT for Q2

payload.comparator: Control arm(s) from the same RCT (usual-timing or CER, per site) with identical objective phenotyping; the comparator for the causal contrast is the randomised fasting vs non-fasting difference before vs after adjustment/mediated decomposition for sleep, late-night intake, and activity.
payload.cost_estimate: Planning assumptions: ~12 months if piggybacked on P1/P2, roughly $150k–$300k incremental (assumption: wearables, actigraphy, food-timing assays, analysis); cheapest per unit of causal information if nested. As a standalone study, roughly $400k–$600k (assumption).
payload.design: Prospectively nested mechanistic/phenotyping study within a fasting RCT (P1- or P2-type design; cheapest informative option is to nest rather than stand alone). Units: participants. Assignment inherits parent randomisation (fasting vs control). All participants receive identical objective monitoring: wrist actigraphy + sleep diaries, continuous glucose monitoring, time-stamped diet photos with late-night intake flagging, and hip/accelerometer physical-activity tracking across run-in and intervention. Timing: baseline 2-week phenotyping, then 12 weeks with repeated 2-week intensive monitoring blocks (assumption). No additional blinding beyond parent trial; analysts of mediation models blinded to arm. Prespecified causal mediation/confounder-adjustment plan separating total effect from natural direct effect of fasting assignment.
payload.falsifier: Q3 (co-behavioural confounding) is refuted if a clinically meaningful fasting effect persists after full adjustment: direct (unmediated) effect still ≥0.4-unit HOMA-IR or ≥10% relative improvement (assumption for smallest important direct effect) with a confidence interval excluding zero. Q3 is supported if adjustment for sleep duration/efficiency, late-night energy intake, and activity attenuates the total fasting effect to below that threshold (near-zero direct effect).
payload.measurements: Primary outcome: same HOMA-IR change as parent trial (central blinded assay). Mediators/confounders measured objectively: actigraphic sleep duration/efficiency and timing; proportion of energy intake after 21:00 (assumption for late-night cut-off) from time-stamped records; daily step count and moderate-to-vigorous activity minutes. Prespecified mediation and confounder-adjusted models with sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding.
payload.risks: Threats: measurement error in behaviours; mediator-outcome confounding despite randomisation of exposure; post-randomisation selection (wearable non-wear); model misspecification; overadjustment for true mediators vs confounders. Ethics/safety: minimal incremental risk (wearables/diaries burden, privacy of timestamped data — de-identified storage and consent, assumption); inherits parent-trial safety monitoring.
payload.sample_size: No new enrolment if nested: full parent-trial sample (e.g., ~140–180, assumptions per P1/P2) with ≥80% valid wear/log time (assumption). Power is for the direct effect after mediation adjustment; all mediation effect-size, correlation, and missing-data inputs are assumptions stated in the analysis plan.
payload.title: P3 nested objective-behaviour mediation study for Q3

payload.decision: Run P3 nested in P1 first (or IPD re-analysis + isocaloric pilot if budget-constrained): recorded evidence shows fasting-associated glycemic improvement (W4400305946, W3098144176, W3194089427) tempered by ITT-null in impaired fasting glucose (W4387263072) and comparable weight effects vs continuous restriction in healthy adults (W4387491927); no source tests isocaloric timing, per-kg, or mediation estimands, so P1 gives the cleanest causal test of timing and nested P3 gives the cheapest discrimination of behavioural vs physiological mechanism.
payload.rationale: Evidence currently suggests modest fasting-associated glycemic improvement but cannot isolate timing from deficit: supports/context W4400305946, W3098144176, W3194089427; contradicts on ITT W4387263072; baseline off-population W4387491927. Q1/Q2/Q3 all untested (posterior 0.5, zero direct tests). P1 isocaloric TRE RCT is the most informative per cost as standalone (isolates timing; falsifier: TRE-minus-control HOMA-IR difference ~0 or CI excludes 15%/0.5-unit threshold); P3 nested in P1 adds mediation at low incremental cost (~$150k-300k) and addresses the key leakage/confounder rival. Conclusion would change if: P1 shows HOMA-IR improvement at equal intake with clamp corroboration (confirm intake-independent effect); or P2 shows residual vanishes after weight adjustment (support Q2); or P3 shows full attenuation via sleep/late-night/activity (support Q3). Critic verdict CONFIRMED: protocols only conditionally falsifying given adherence/measurement/identification assumptions; prespecify single ITT primary and re-justify thresholds from observed variances.
